title: REST APIs In Depth
summary: Resources, HTTP methods, CRUD, and status codes — the full picture.
heading: REST APIs In Depth

blocks.text: Back in the taste chapter we saw that a REST API is a set of web addresses your app calls to get and send data. Now let's go deeper: how those addresses are organised, which HTTP method to use, and what the server's reply means.

blocks.label: Revisit Chapter 11: A Taste of REST and fetch

blocks.text: REST is built around resources — things like users, products, or posts. Each resource has a collection address and an item address.

cards.title: Single item
cards.code:
/users/1       the user with id 1
/products/42   the product with id 42

blocks.text: Use plural nouns for collections (/users), and put the id in the path for one item (/users/1) — not verbs like /getUser.
The four basic data operations — Create, Read, Update, Delete (CRUD) — map directly onto four HTTP methods.

layers.title: GET
layers.detail: Read — fetch a collection or one item (never changes data)

layers.title: POST
layers.detail: Create — add a new item to a collection

layers.title: PUT
layers.detail: Update — replace an existing item with new data

blocks.label: CRUD on /users
blocks.code:
GET    /users        -> list users      (Read)
GET    /users/1      -> one user        (Read)
POST   /users        -> create a user    (Create)
PUT    /users/1      -> update user 1    (Update)
DELETE /users/1      -> remove user 1    (Delete)

blocks.text: GET asks for data and never changes anything. It has no request body — everything it needs is in the URL. The server replies with 200 OK and the data.
GET is safe (changes nothing) and idempotent (asking twice gives the same answer), so results can be cached.
POST sends new data in the request body to a collection. The server creates the item, assigns it an id, and replies with 201 Created and the new item.
POST is not idempotent: send it twice and you create two items. You POST to the collection (/users), not to an id.
PUT replaces an existing item at its id with the full object you send. The server applies it and replies with 200 OK and the updated item.
PUT is idempotent: sending the same update again leaves the item in the same state. Send the whole object — fields you leave out can be wiped.
DELETE removes the item at its id. It usually needs no body, and the server often replies with 204 No Content (success, nothing to return).
DELETE is idempotent: once the item is gone, deleting it again still ends with it gone (often a 404 the second time).
A request has a method, a URL, optional headers (extra info like the data format or an auth token), and — for POST and PUT — a body with the data.

blocks.label: POST /users
blocks.code:
POST /users HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "name": "Asha",
  "age": 20
}

blocks.text: The server replies with a status code and usually a body (often JSON).
The status code tells you what happened. The first digit is the family.

layers.title: 2xx — Success
layers.detail: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content (e.g. after DELETE)

layers.title: 4xx — Your request was wrong
layers.detail: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: 2xx = it worked, 4xx = fix your request, 5xx = the server has a problem.
Two handy ideas: a safe method doesn't change data (GET). An idempotent method gives the same result no matter how many times you repeat it.

items: PUT and DELETE — idempotent (repeating gives the same end state).
POST — not idempotent (calling it twice creates two items).
REST is organised around resources: /users and /users/1.
CRUD maps to methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.
Requests carry a method, URL, headers, and (sometimes) a body.
Status codes: 2xx success, 4xx your fault, 5xx server's fault.
GET is safe; PUT/DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.
